con:
Thank you for participating in our survey on prosecutorial approaches. As a person with expertise on criminal matters, your professional assessment is invaluable to our understanding of prosecutorial trends.



We are seeking expert opinions on where elected prosecutors fall on the spectrum, ranging from traditional to progressive, in their approach to criminal justice. Your familiarity with the prosecutorial landscape makes your perspective particularly valuable for this research.



Your participation will take approximately 10 minutes. There are no risks associated with this study.



If you have read this form and have decided to participate in this project, please understand your participation is voluntary and you have the right to withdraw your consent or discontinue participation at any time without penalty or loss of benefits to which you are otherwise entitled. The alternative is not to participate. You have the right to refuse to answer particular questions. The results of this research study may be presented at scientific or professional meetings or published in scientific journals. Your individual privacy will be maintained in all published and written data resulting from the study.



If you have any questions, concerns or complaints about this research, its procedures, risks and benefits, contact Dvir Yogev, The Criminal Law and Justice Center, UC Berkeley, dyo@berkeley.edu, CPHS Protocol ID: 2023-03-16211, or Carissa Byrne Hessick, The Prosecutors and Politics Project, University of North Carolina School of Law, chessick@email.unc.edu IRB Study # 25-1888.



By clicking “Agree,” you indicate your consent to take part in the survey.
def:
This survey uses the term “traditional prosecutors” to refer to those prosecutors who tend to emphasize conviction rates and punitive sentences, and it uses the term “progressive prosecutors” to refer to those prosecutors who tend to focus on diversion and rehabilitation. 
We recognize that most prosecutors incorporate elements of both approaches, and our interest is in understanding the spectrum of prosecutorial ideology.

If you have any related notes on how you understand these concepts, please insert them below.

Q54:
The term progressive prosecutor is defined very differently depending on who is using it and for what purpose. At times, it can be weaponized as a label—either as a criticism or as a badge of honor—without much clarity. In my opinion, the label in its most useful and positive sense is defined by an effort to advance and experiment with alternatives to the traditional adjudicative system. That can mean creating or expanding diversion opportunities, designing dispositions that focus on treatment rather than punishment while also ensuring strong oversight and accountability in programs, and supporting individuals who are working to change the trajectory of their lives.

At the same time, I think it is important to acknowledge that the term can carry a more negative connotation when it is used to justify sweeping declination policies that categorically avoid prosecuting entire types of crime. When applied too broadly, such approaches can have real consequences for community members, undermine public trust, and diminish the effectiveness of diversion programs that otherwise show real promise.

To me, the value of “progressive” prosecution lies in thoughtful innovation—using data, evidence, and compassion to expand options beyond the traditional adjudicative and sentencing models—while still ensuring accountability and protecting the communities we serve.

I think the term "progressive" prosecutor is thrown around/ill-defined, in modern times. There is little in common, for example, with prosecutors in Larry Krazner's office (when he took office, he decreed drug possession cases would not be prosecuted) and so-called "progressive" prosecutors, either elected, or line, who do prosecute drug-possession; who will not dismiss those cases; and who insist on some kind of plea-offers with probation, treatment, etc. 

The latter may call themselves "progressive" but that is anything-but; I point it out simply to make the point that in my mind, actual, so-called "progressive" prosecutors not only employ evidence-based practices/are intellectually honest and consistent, with regards to their practices, but do not prosecute cases like drug possession, and do not prosecute cases that have insufficient evidence.

Rather than focusing solely on securing convictions or imposing harsh sentences, they prioritize reducing incarceration, addressing racial and economic disparities, and promoting alternatives that foster rehabilitation and community safety. def:
I am pretty skeptical of the progressive prosecutor label.  That's in part because I think that (consistent with the note above) prosecutors tend to incorporate a range of different positions into their platform or approach. From my perspective, though, it’s interesting which of those features each of us finds most memorable/salient and how to distinguish between what we identify as the defining or characteristic policies, and which we define as outlier policies.  For example, Mike Doherty in Boulder got a lot of attention for certain diversion practices and also an emphasis on progressive targets (e.g., wage theft).  On the other hand, his opposition to drug decriminalization, opposition to clemency efforts, and continued prosecutions for illegal camping all strike me as traditional.  My intuition, though, is that if you asked most people in CO, they’d say he was progressive.  Of course, part of that might just be cultural (i.e., people tend to perceive Boulder as very progressive).  But part of it might be that the issues that struck people as newsworthy put him in the progressive bucket.  I think you could tell a similar story about most prosecutors that might cut in either direction (e.g., the prosecutor whose office isn’t actually aggressive about seeking pretrial detention, but rarely agrees to diversion).  

I am wary of pretending that I understand or have any great insight into electoral politics—and, I am even warier when discussing a jurisdiction where I don’t (and haven’t) lived.  But I wonder whether part of Krasner’s success actually has to do with his mastery of this dynamic: Krasner hasn’t been shy about taking high-salience progressive positions, but he also hasn’t been shy about acting very much like a “traditional” prosecutor on newsworthy issues (e.g., his statements about homicides and gun violence cases).

def:
At this point, I think of "progressive prosecutor" more as a political identity label than as anything with substantive content. At the outset (circa 2015-17), it denoted a prosecutor who was striving to take a more holistic approach to prosecution than their predecessors and to reduce the footprint of the criminal justice system, including by reducing incarceration and probation rates and rates of pretrial detention on low cash bail (overall - to reduce pointless incarceration and supervision). But ten years into a nationwide sea change in criminal justice discourse and practice, there's no longer as clear a prosecutorial baseline as there was in 2015.  So some prosecutors identify as, or are called, "progressive prosecutors" who are just as punitive as most others; and some prosecutors are moving their jurisdiction quite dramatically toward a more holistic approach, but don't think of themselves as - and aren't called - "progressive prosecutors." 

Basically, I think most urban prosecutors these days are doing the same kinds of things, and they're all doing things that we called "progressive" five years ago. So I try not to use the term anymore and instead to talk about specific policy challenges and policy approaches.

Q54:
A progressive prosecutor is one who redefines the role of prosecution by prioritizing fairness, equity, and community well-being over maximizing convictions and incarceration. Their policies often include declining to prosecute low-level offenses, seeking alternatives to jail such as diversion or restorative justice programs, and eliminating cash bail to prevent wealth-based detention. They also emphasize proportionality in sentencing, favor rehabilitation and reintegration, and revisit past cases involving excessive sentences or bias through conviction review units. These approaches reflect a broader goal of reducing reliance on incarceration and addressing the criminalization of poverty, substance use, mental illness, and homelessness.

Equally important, progressive prosecutors acknowledge and work to counteract the racial and social inequities deeply embedded in the criminal legal system. They promote transparency by publishing office data and policies, engage with communities through advisory boards, and pursue accountability for law enforcement misconduct. Beyond the courtroom, they advocate for systemic reforms such as abolishing mandatory minimums or the death penalty and support broader decriminalization efforts. At its core, progressive prosecution reframes the prosecutor’s role: instead of centering punishment, it seeks to minimize harm, repair relationships, and pursue safety through equity and social supports rather than incarceration.

Q54:
In my mind, the primary value/approach that characterizes progressive prosecution is a focus on non-carceral outcomes. For example, trying alternative forms of supervised release: traditional probation can be complicated, even for the most well-meaning, and the requirements are often out of reach for indigent defendants. My understanding is that some jurisdictions have other forms of supervised release that are better suited to help people. In my jurisdiction, traditional probation is often the only option available to avoid a carceral sentence.  

Substance abuse and mental health treatment programs are certainly the ideal outcome for many defendants, where they may get the chance to address the root cause of their behavior. Obviously, an issue is that these programs are chronically underfunded, and convincing traditional funding sources (typically governments) to put more resources here is a challenge. This is where I think another line is drawn between "progressive" prosecutors and traditional ones, whether they'll advocate for these programs directly to funding sources. Many prosecutors are willing to use the available resources, but I don't think we often see prosecutors going to the funding sources and advocating for more resources to be allocated to treatment programs.
